items.explanation: The corruption charge was partisan advocacy in the first party fight, not a neutral finding -- it came from Jeffersonian opponents of Hamilton in an emerging struggle over the government's direction. A historian must identify who was speaking and what they hoped to gain before treating the charge as proof; assuming the founders' virtue, taking the critics' rhetoric about farmers at face value, or recasting a policy dispute as personal graft all skip that step.
items.fact_source: Hamilton's First Report on Public Credit (January 1790) proposed federal assumption of state debts and funding at face value; critics charged it rewarded speculators; the plan passed in the Compromise of 1790.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Assuming leaders like Hamilton always acted for the public good replaces investigation with hero worship; motives must be examined, not assumed.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. That the critics attacked the plan in the farmers' name does not prove farmers supported Hamilton's program -- the critics' rhetoric is not evidence of farmers' views.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The charge was that speculators who bought certificates cheaply would profit, not that Hamilton enriched himself personally; and the charge itself came from partisan opponents.
option_explanations.D: Right. Recognizing the critics' partisan point of view is the necessary first step in evaluating their charge.

options: (A) must be false, because leaders like Hamilton consistently placed the nation's interest above personal or factional gain
(B) shows that ordinary farmers supported Hamilton's program, because the critics attacked it in the farmers' name
(C) proves Hamilton designed the plan mainly to enrich himself personally
(D) came from Jeffersonian opponents in an emerging partisan struggle over the government's direction
items.stem: A historian quoting the critics' charge as proof that Hamilton's plan was corrupt should first consider that the charge

stimulus.text: In 1790 Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton proposed that the federal government assume state debts and fund the national debt at face value. Critics charged that the plan would enrich speculators who had bought up debt certificates cheaply from soldiers and farmers.

items.explanation: The French government was an absolute monarchy, and Vergennes pursued the alliance to weaken Britain and avenge the Seven Years' War -- a strategic motive, not republican sympathy. Volunteers' feelings do not explain a monarchy's foreign policy, one battle's timing does not identify the motive, and the 1789 Revolution cannot be projected backward onto 1778.
items.fact_source: The Treaty of Alliance was signed February 6, 1778; Foreign Minister Vergennes pursued the alliance to weaken Britain after the Seven Years' War, committing only after Saratoga (October 1777) demonstrated American viability (see Jonathan Dull, A Diplomatic History of the American Revolution).

option_explanations.A: Right. An absolute monarchy allied to avenge its defeat and weaken its rival -- that strategic motive, not sympathy for republican ideals, explains the French state's decision.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lafayette's admiration was real, but individual volunteers' feelings cannot be generalized into the French government's motive for allying.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Saratoga's timing fits a strategic motive, but one battle's timing alone does not identify the motive -- France waited for proof of viability before committing.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. This projects the French Revolution of 1789 backward; nothing in 1778 shows French leaders favored replacing their monarchy with a republic.

options: (A) France was an absolute monarchy seeking revenge on Britain for the Seven Years' War -- a strategic motive, not republican sympathy
(B) French volunteers such as Lafayette genuinely admired the American cause, which shows the French government shared their republican ideals
(C) France signed only after the victory at Saratoga, which proves the American battlefield success alone caused the alliance
(D) The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy, which shows French leaders already favored republican government when they signed the alliance in 1778
items.stem: A student claims that France signed the 1778 Treaty of Alliance mainly because French leaders sympathized with American republican ideals. Which consideration most weakens this claim?

items.explanation: Gradual abolition meant most enslaved people in the North stayed bound for decades -- Pennsylvania's 1780 law freed only the future children of enslaved mothers, and only at age twenty-eight. One founder's will, the Declaration's promise, and modern moral judgments are not evidence about the pace at which slavery ended.
items.fact_source: Pennsylvania's Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery (1780) freed only the future children of enslaved mothers, upon reaching age twenty-eight.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Washington's will freed the people he enslaved, but one famous man's decision does not show how quickly slavery ended across the new nation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Declaration's promise that all men are created equal states an ideal; a promise is not evidence that slavery ended soon after it was signed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Judging the founders by twenty-first-century standards evaluates their morals; it is not evidence about the pace at which slavery ended.
option_explanations.D: Right. The law's gradual terms directly contradict 'rapidly ended,' showing liberty arrived slowly and unevenly.

options: (A) George Washington freed the people he enslaved in his will, which shows slavery was ending quickly across the new nation
(B) The Declaration of Independence promised that all men are created equal, which means slavery must have ended soon after it was signed
(C) By the standards of the twenty-first century, the founders' views on race were prejudiced, which proves slavery continued
(D) Pennsylvania's 1780 law freed only children born to enslaved mothers, and only after they served to age twenty-eight
items.stem: A student argues: 'The Revolution's promise of liberty rapidly ended slavery in the new nation.' Which evidence would most challenge this argument?

items.explanation: Independence ended the Proclamation of 1763's restraint on western settlement, and states and speculators rushed to claim and sell western lands -- that is what dates the wave to the 1780s and 1790s. Fertile soil alone cannot explain the timing, statehood followed settlement rather than causing it, and a timeless 'frontier spirit' would push Americans west in every decade, not this one in particular.
items.fact_source: Kentucky (1792) and Tennessee (1796) achieved statehood after rapid postwar settlement; the Proclamation of 1763's western barrier ended with independence, and states ceded or sold western land claims to speculators and settlers.

option_explanations.A: Right. The war's end removed the British barrier and unleashed the state and speculative land claims that drew settlers west in exactly these decades.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The bluegrass was fertile long before the 1780s; good soil alone cannot explain why the settlement wave happened when it did.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This reverses cause and effect -- rapid settlement produced the population that made statehood possible, not the other way around.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A restless love of wilderness may describe frontier culture, but a timeless spirit cannot explain why the surge happened in the 1780s and 1790s rather than any other decade.

options: (A) Independence ended British limits on western settlement, opening lands that states and speculators rushed to sell
(B) The rich soil of the Kentucky bluegrass drew farmers west, and good land alone explains why settlement happened when it did
(C) Kentucky and Tennessee became states in the 1790s, and the promise of statehood drew settlers across the mountains
(D) A restless frontier spirit -- love of wilderness and individualism -- pushed Americans west in the 1780s just as it had in every earlier generation
items.stem: What best explains the rapid settlement of Kentucky and Tennessee in the 1780s and 1790s?

items.explanation: Both essays appeal to liberty and the British constitution; the real disagreement is over where liberty is safe. One essayist does not speak for most colonists, a sincere Loyalist argument is not a defense of tyranny, and an anonymous essay's content still counts as evidence of Loyalist thinking.
items.fact_source: Daniel Leonard's 'Massachusettensis' essays (1774-75) defended Parliament's authority; John Adams answered as 'Novanglus' (1775), defending colonial resistance. Both appealed to liberty and the British constitution.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. One Patriot essayist's argument does not prove what most colonists believed by 1775; a single writer cannot stand in for the whole population.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. This caricatures the Loyalist position -- Leonard sincerely argued that lawful Parliamentary authority protected colonial liberty, a view many colonists held.
option_explanations.C: Right. Both appeal to liberty, and their disagreement turns on whether Parliament is liberty's guardian or its enemy.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That Leonard wrote anonymously does not erase what his essays argue; historians treat them as genuine evidence of Loyalist thinking.

options: (A) The Patriot essay proves that most colonists had already rejected British authority by 1775
(B) The Patriot writer defends liberty while the Loyalist writer defends submission to tyranny
(C) Both writers claim to defend liberty, but disagree about whether Parliament's authority threatens it or protects it
(D) Because Leonard wrote anonymously, his essay cannot be treated as a genuine statement of Loyalist thinking in the colonies
items.stem: Which comparison of the two arguments is most accurate?

stimulus.text: Source 1 -- John Adams, writing as 'Novanglus' (1775): Parliament's claim to tax the colonies without their consent reduces free subjects toward slavery; resistance is therefore lawful self-defense. Source 2 -- Daniel Leonard, writing as 'Massachusettensis' (1775): Parliament's authority is lawful and supreme; resistance is rebellion that will destroy the liberty colonists enjoy under the British constitution.

items.explanation: If the laws were purely about wartime security, enforcement would not have fallen only on the opposition press -- the one-sided prosecutions reveal a partisan purpose behind the security justification. Expiration dates, the foreign crisis, and the laws' harshness do not by themselves establish that purpose.
items.fact_source: Sedition Act prosecutions in 1798-1800 (including that of Congressman Matthew Lyon) fell on Democratic-Republican editors and politicians; the Federalist press was not prosecuted.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. That the acts expired on schedule is consistent with either a security or a partisan motive -- a later expiration does not reveal the original purpose.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Quasi-War explains the timing, but it cannot by itself rule out a second motive; one cause does not exclude the partisan pattern in how the laws were enforced.
option_explanations.C: Right. Selective prosecution of Republican editors is the strongest evidence that partisan advantage, not just security, drove the acts.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. This projects a modern absolutist idea of free speech onto 1798; the harshness of the laws does not by itself prove their purpose was purely partisan or purely security-driven.

options: (A) The acts were allowed to expire within a few years of passage, which proves they were intended only as temporary wartime security
(B) The Quasi-War with France fully explains the acts, since foreign crises are the only reason governments pass security laws
(C) Only Republican editors were prosecuted under the Sedition Act; Federalist critics of the government went unpunished
(D) The acts punished criticism of the government, which proves the Federalists rejected the idea of free speech entirely
items.stem: A student claims the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 were purely wartime security measures prompted by the Quasi-War with France. Which evidence most undermines this claim?

items.explanation: The 1765 petitions professed loyalty to the king and demanded the rights of English subjects within the empire; the turn toward independence came later, after further conflicts. Reading later independence back into 1765, generalizing from militants to the whole population, or treating the petitions' formal tone as proof of mild feeling all miss what the petitions actually said.
items.fact_source: The Stamp Act Congress's Declaration of Rights and Grievances (October 1765) professed 'due subordination' to Parliament while denying its right to tax the colonies.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The militant actions of the Sons of Liberty do not show what the whole colonial population wanted -- and fierce protest against a tax is not the same as a commitment to independence.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. That independence came eleven years later does not prove the 1765 petitions began the drive for it; a later outcome cannot supply an earlier intent.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Petitions are written in formal language as a matter of genre; the tone of the document is not a measure of how seriously the petitioners pressed their constitutional claims.
option_explanations.D: Right. The petitions' language of loyalty and rights within the empire contradicts the claim of an existing commitment to independence.

options: (A) is supported, because the street actions of the Sons of Liberty -- burning stamps and hanging tax collectors in effigy -- show the colonies as a whole had turned toward independence
(B) is supported, because independence came only eleven years later, which shows the 1765 petitions were the first step toward separation
(C) is undermined, because the petitions were written in polite and formal language, which shows the colonists were not deeply upset with Parliament
(D) is undermined, because the petitions professed loyalty to the king and demanded the rights of English subjects within the empire rather than separation from it
items.stem: A student writes in an essay: 'The petitions of the Stamp Act Congress in 1765 prove that the colonists were already committed to independence that year.' Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

items.explanation: Qualifying means adding what the simple story leaves out. The 1780 act was real progress — the first such law in America — but 'ended slavery' overstates it badly: a person enslaved in 1779 died enslaved. Revolutionary ideals helped make the law possible, Quaker activism pushed it, and economic and political interests watered it down. The honest claim is that the Revolution began slavery's slow retreat in the North, not that it finished the job.
items.fact_source: Pennsylvania Gradual Abolition Act, March 1, 1780: children born to enslaved mothers after that date were freed at age 28; those already enslaved remained enslaved for life; similar gradual laws followed in other northern states. College Board CED topic 3.6.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The law's own terms — no immediate freedom, lifetime bondage for those already enslaved, decades of labor owed by their children — qualify the student's claim into a more accurate one about gradual change.
option_explanations.B: This overcorrects. The law was a genuine, ideals-driven breakthrough and a model for other northern states; saying the Revolution changed nothing ignores the gradual abolition movement it helped start.
option_explanations.C: The law's supporters invoked the Revolution's ideals of liberty; gradualism reflected political and economic compromise with slaveholding interests, not rejection of the ideals.
option_explanations.D: Quaker activism mattered, but single-cause explanations fail here: revolutionary rhetoric, wartime service by Black soldiers, and economic calculation all shaped the law. 'Only' is the giveaway.

options: (A) The law freed no one immediately: those already enslaved stayed enslaved for life, and their children still owed decades of labor — the Revolution started a slow process, not an ending.
(B) The law proves that revolutionary ideals changed nothing at all about slavery anywhere in America, in the North or the South, in 1780 or in any later year.
(C) The law shows that Pennsylvania's leaders rejected the Revolution's ideals.

(D) The law was caused only by Quaker religious beliefs and had nothing to do with the Revolution, its ideals, the wartime service of Black soldiers, or the changing economic interests of Pennsylvania.
items.stem: A student argues that the American Revolution ended slavery in Pennsylvania. Which consideration best qualifies this claim?

stimulus.text: Pennsylvania's 1780 law for the gradual abolition of slavery declared children born to enslaved mothers after its passage free upon reaching age twenty-eight, while people already enslaved remained enslaved for life.

items.explanation: Calling the Ordinance simply 'antislavery' leaves out what the law itself did for slavery: its fugitive clause ordered the return of escapees as property, and settlers used long-term indentures to keep bound Black labor in the region anyway. A ban with built-in protections for slaveholders needs a qualifier, not a slogan. (A) overcredits one law -- the region's free-labor future also depended on settlers, migration, and economics. (C) imagines a united founding generation that did not exist; the same era's Constitution protected the slave trade until 1808. (D) goes too far the other way: the ban genuinely shaped how the Northwest developed.
items.fact_source: Northwest Ordinance, Article VI (1787): 'There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the said territory,' with a proviso for reclaiming fugitive laborers; long-term indentures persisted in Indiana and Illinois into the nineteenth century. College Board CED topic 3.12.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This gives one statute the whole credit. The Northwest's development as free territory also depended on who settled there, migration patterns, and economics -- not on a single law alone.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The fugitive provision and the persistence of bound Black labor through indentures show that the anti-slavery ban coexisted with concrete protections for slavery -- the evidence that complicates the simple label.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The same generation wrote a Constitution that barred Congress from touching the slave trade until 1808. The Ordinance reflects a divided, compromising generation, not a united one.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The ban had real consequences: it shaped the Northwest's development as free territory. Loopholes weakened it, but 'no real effect' ignores how the region actually developed.

options: (A) The Ordinance alone created the Northwest as free territory, so this one federal law was the single decisive force behind the region's development.
(B) The Ordinance's own fugitive provision treated escapees as property to be returned, and long-term indentures kept bound Black labor in the region for decades.
(C) The Ordinance proves the founding generation was united in opposing slavery, sharing one antislavery purpose, one program, and one timetable for bringing it to an end.

(D) The Ordinance had no real effect because western settlers simply ignored the ban entirely, holding enslaved people openly without consequence -- making the famous prohibition a dead letter from the start.
items.stem: A historian calls the Ordinance 'the first federal law against slavery.' Which evidence most complicates that description?

stimulus.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 prohibited slavery in the territory northwest of the Ohio River.

items.explanation: Both pamphlets speak the same constitutional language -- consent, natural rights, the rights of Englishmen -- and use it to reach opposite conclusions about Parliament's power. The fight is over what those shared principles require in the colonies' case, not over whether liberty matters. (A) gets the history backwards: nobody here invents a philosophy from scratch, and the Loyalist is arguing constitutional law, not blind obedience. (C) caricatures Loyalists as enemies of liberty; Source 2 shows the Loyalist insisting colonists already possess English rights. (D) shrinks a genuine dispute over consent and representation into a mere misunderstanding.
items.fact_source: Colonial pamphlets (e.g., Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer, 1767-68; Jefferson's Summary View, 1774) invoked Locke and English constitutional rights; Loyalist writers such as Daniel Leonard (Massachusettensis, 1774-75) answered within the same constitutional vocabulary, defending virtual representation. College Board CED topic 3.4.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Neither pamphlet invents a philosophy from nothing, and the Loyalist is making a constitutional argument about representation, not preaching blind obedience to whatever Parliament decrees.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Both sources appeal to the same tradition -- English constitutionalism and natural rights -- and reach opposite conclusions because they disagree about how its principles apply to the colonies' situation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This caricatures Loyalists as opponents of liberty itself. Source 2 shows the Loyalist claiming colonists already enjoy the rights of Englishmen; the dispute is over what those rights require, not whether liberty matters.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The sources show a real dispute over consent and representation, not a trivial mix-up. Disagreeing about the application of a principle is still disagreeing about something important.

options: (A) The colonial pamphlet invents a brand-new philosophy of rights out of nothing, while the Loyalist pamphlet simply defends obeying whatever Parliament decrees.
(B) Both pamphlets argue from the same English constitutional tradition, but they disagree about how its principles apply to the colonies' situation.
(C) The Loyalist pamphlet shows that Loyalists opposed liberty itself and wanted the colonies ruled as conquered subjects with no rights at all.
(D) The two pamphlets agree on every important principle and differ only on small details of tax policy, so the whole crisis was basically a misunderstanding.
items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between the two arguments?

stimulus.text:
Source 1 -- A 1774 colonial pamphlet argues that a Parliament in which the colonies have no representatives cannot justly tax them, since government rests on the consent of the governed and a people may resist rulers who violate their natural rights.

Source 2 -- A 1775 Loyalist pamphlet replies that colonists already enjoy the full rights of Englishmen because Parliament represents the whole empire, and that resisting lawful taxes is rebellion against that constitution.

items.explanation: Brutus was campaigning, not summarizing. His job was to frighten readers into rejecting the Constitution, so he read the clause in the most alarming way possible. That makes the essay excellent evidence of what Anti-Federalists feared and how they argued — and poor evidence of what the clause 'really meant,' a question the Federalists answered very differently and the courts took decades to settle.
items.fact_source: The Brutus essays (1787–88, likely written by Robert Yates) attacked the necessary and proper clause and the supremacy clause as engines of consolidated power; Federalists (notably Hamilton in Federalist 33) replied that the clause granted no powers beyond those already enumerated. College Board CED topic 3.8.

option_explanations.A: This mistakes a critic's worst-case reading for the authors' intent. Brutus opposed the Constitution; his alarm about the clause tells us about his fears, not about what the framers meant to authorize.
option_explanations.B: What later generations did with the clause — McCulloch v. Maryland came in 1819 — cannot confirm what anyone intended in 1787. Later use is a different historical question from original meaning.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Sourcing asks what a document can and cannot show: Brutus's purpose (defeat ratification) and audience (wavering voters) make his essay strong evidence of Anti-Federalist argument and weak evidence of the clause's settled legal meaning.
option_explanations.D: The Anti-Federalists feared that a distant, powerful central government would resemble monarchy; they wanted power kept in the states. They did not favor monarchy itself.

options: (A) It proves that the framers intended Congress to exercise unlimited power under the clause, sweeping aside every limit the Constitution appears to set.
(B) It is confirmed because the federal government later used the clause to justify broad powers, which proves Brutus correctly grasped the framers' true and original design from the very start.
(C) It is evidence of Anti-Federalist fears and persuasion tactics during ratification — Brutus wrote to defeat ratification, so his alarming reading must be weighed against Federalist replies.
(D) It shows the Anti-Federalists opposed the Constitution because they actually favored monarchy and wanted a king ruling America rather than any republican government at all.
items.stem: Which statement best evaluates Brutus's warning as historical evidence?

stimulus.text: In a 1787 Anti-Federalist essay, 'Brutus' warns that the Constitution's necessary and proper clause will let Congress claim unlimited power, sweeping away every right the states have reserved.

items.explanation: France was an absolute monarchy that feared republican ideas at home; it bankrolled the American revolution to avenge its 1763 defeat and cripple Britain, with American trade as a bonus. Saratoga mattered because it showed the rebellion could survive -- the war still had four years to run. (A) reads later ideals into a king's foreign policy. (B) shrinks a great-power decision to one man's charm. (C) confuses a promising sign with a certain outcome.
items.fact_source: The Treaty of Alliance was signed in February 1778, after Saratoga (October 1777); French foreign minister Vergennes sought to avenge France's Seven Years' War losses and weaken Britain, with commercial access to America as a further prize. College Board CED topic 3.5.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. This reads later ideals back into an absolute monarchy. France's government opposed republicanism at home; its motives were strategic -- weakening Britain -- not ideological.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Franklin's diplomacy helped, but no one man's popularity explains a great-power alliance. France acted on its own strategic interests, not on charm.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. In early 1778 nothing was certain; Britain still held New York and would campaign for years. Saratoga persuaded France the Americans were a worthwhile bet, not a guaranteed winner.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Placing the alliance inside the long Bourbon-British rivalry explains what ideology cannot: why an absolute monarchy bankrolled a republican revolution -- to avenge its Seven Years' War defeat and break British power.

options: (A) France's dedication to spreading republican government, which the American cause embodied -- the alliance was an ideological crusade for liberty and shared revolutionary principles above all else.
(B) Benjamin Franklin's personal popularity in Paris, which charmed the French court into gambling on the rebellion regardless of France's own interests.
(C) France's certainty after Saratoga that American victory was now inevitable, which made the alliance a risk-free move to share in the spoils.
(D) France's rivalry with Britain: humiliated by its Seven Years' War defeat, France seized the chance to weaken its old enemy once Saratoga proved the Americans could win.
items.stem: After the American victory at Saratoga in 1777, France signed treaties of alliance and commerce with the United States. Which broader context best explains France's decision?

items.explanation: The memorandum treats 'the colonies' as a single economy, but the war's costs and profits fell very unevenly. Port-city merchants and army contractors grew rich, while Pennsylvania's frontier absorbed devastating raids. The deeper flaw is not that taxes followed the war — they did — but that the argument builds its case on a false picture of shared colonial prosperity. Colonial objections, meanwhile, centered on Parliament's authority to tax at all, not on the size of the bill.
items.fact_source: Britain's national debt roughly doubled during the Seven Years' War (to about £133 million); Grenville's revenue program (Sugar Act 1764, Stamp Act 1765) sought colonial contributions toward imperial defense costs; wartime contracting enriched merchants in port cities while frontier regions suffered raids and occupation. College Board CED topic 3.2.

option_explanations.A: This accepts the memorandum's premise without examining it. Sound evaluation requires checking whether the evidence — here, the claim that the colonies as a whole grew rich — actually supports the conclusion.
option_explanations.B: This confuses sequence with explanation: the fact that taxes followed the war does not by itself prove why they were imposed. It also misstates colonial objections, which were about Parliament's right to tax, not the amounts.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The argument overgeneralizes from the experience of some merchants and contractors to all colonists, ignoring the very different wartime experience of frontier regions. A premise that is false for large parts of the colonies cannot carry the conclusion.
option_explanations.D: This gets the history backwards: Britain bore enormous war costs and even reimbursed some colonial expenses; the colonies did not self-fund the war. The revenue acts were fiscal measures to service debt, not punishments for disloyalty.

options: (A) It is sound: Britain's war debt made new taxes necessary, and the colonies' wartime profits show they could afford to pay their fair share of the empire's costs.

(B) It is sound because taxation always follows a major war, so the colonists' objections must really have been about the size of the tax bills rather than about Parliament's authority to impose them at all.
(C) It is flawed: wartime profits went mostly to coastal merchants and contractors, while frontier regions endured raids and occupation — the premise of uniform colonial enrichment does not hold.

(D) It is sound: colonial assemblies had already paid for the entire war effort out of their own treasuries, so the new taxes were clearly meant to punish colonial disloyalty rather than to raise needed revenue.
items.stem: Which of the following best evaluates the reasoning of the memorandum's argument?

stimulus.text: A 1763 memorandum from a British treasury official argues that because the war left Britain deeply in debt, the colonies — which had grown rich from wartime contracts and trade — should now help pay the empire's costs through new parliamentary taxes.

items.explanation: The essay is a pep talk, not a history lesson — its job is to keep merchants from breaking ranks, so it presents the boycott as an all-powerful weapon. Nonimportation did matter: it squeezed British exporters, who pressured Parliament. But the 1766 repeal also came from a new Rockingham ministry eager to undo Grenville's policies. Treating the boycott as the sole cause, or as proof of economic independence, reads a sales pitch as a complete explanation.
items.fact_source: The Stamp Act was repealed in March 1766 after colonial protest, nonimportation pressure on British merchants, and the Rockingham ministry's replacement of Grenville; the Townshend duties (1767) followed the same pattern of protest and partial retreat. College Board CED topic 3.3.

option_explanations.A: This takes the essay's boast at face value and assigns a single cause to a multi-causal event. The boycott contributed, but British merchant lobbying and the fall of Grenville's ministry were also decisive.
option_explanations.B: A boycott is a pressure tactic, not proof of independence — its very purpose was to inflict pain through the existing trade relationship. Reading the rhetoric literally mistakes a weapon for a description of the economy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Recognizing the essay as persuasion aimed at a specific audience (merchants wavering on the boycott) reveals its limits as evidence: it simplifies a complex repeal into a single heroic cause to keep its readers committed.
option_explanations.D: This is factually wrong. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 and most of the Townshend duties in 1770, both under colonial pressure. The error is in the history, not just the reasoning.

options: (A) The claim is accurate: the colonial boycott alone forced Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act in 1766, with British merchants and the new Rockingham ministry playing no real part whatsoever in that decision or its timing.
(B) The claim proves that the colonies had already become economically independent of Britain by 1768, needing neither British goods nor British markets to thrive.

(C) The essay is written to persuade merchants to stay in the boycott, and it oversimplifies history: the 1766 repeal also reflected lobbying by British merchants hurt by the boycott and a change of ministry in London.
(D) The claim is false because Parliament never repealed any colonial tax in response to colonial pressure, either in 1766 or at any later date.
items.stem: Considering the author's purpose and historical situation, which statement best evaluates the essay's claim?

stimulus.text: A 1768 Boston newspaper essay urging merchants to keep up the nonimportation boycott of British goods declares: 'Parliament understands only the language of trade. Our last refusal bent them; this one will break them.'
